storm.summary_layperson: A round of strong-to-severe thunderstorms is tracking toward the area this afternoon under an active Severe Thunderstorm Watch, but the cool Long Island Sound should weaken or slow storms crossing it before they reach the cove — at least through early evening.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Marine layer is strong right now (12°F air–water gap) and should still be buffering the storm cell tracking in around 4 PM, but the gap narrows fast as the air cools after midday heat peaks and crosses the ~5°F threshold around 7:51 PM — no real buffer left for anything arriving after sunset.
storm.detail_html:
A Severe Thunderstorm Watch is in effect for the region through 8 PM, and radar shows a cluster of cells 14–34 miles to the WNW/NW/NNW, the strongest reaching 53 dBZ. Instability is high (CAPE 2,030 J/kg) with strong deep-layer shear (28.6 kt), the kind of environment that supports organized, potentially severe storms — consistent with the NWS Upton forecast discussion's mention of MLCAPE over 2,000 J/kg and isolated-to-scattered severe storms into the evening.

The nearest cell is 14 miles WNW, closing at 23 kt, with a radar-based arrival window of roughly 4:09 PM (range 3:59–4:26 PM). Long Island Sound is running about 76°F against 88°F air — a 12°F gap — which supports a moderate marine stable layer. The Sound holds its temperature while the air over land keeps heating, so a cool, dense layer sits over the water; storms crossing it from the WNW (a near-perpendicular approach) tend to weaken or run late as they cross. That buffer is still fully intact for the 4 PM cell.

The catch is that the buffer decays through the afternoon and evening as air temperatures fall back from their midday peak. The 12°F gap now narrows to roughly 7°F by 7 PM and drops below the ~5°F threshold around 7:51 PM as the Sound stays flat near 76°F but the air cools toward the mid-70s after sunset. Anything crossing the Sound before roughly 7:45 PM still gets a meaningful discount; anything arriving after that should be treated as arriving at full strength.

Net call: the cove and immediate shoreline should see a somewhat weaker or later version of what inland Westchester and northern Fairfield County get this afternoon and early evening, particularly the ~4 PM cell. There are more cells stacked farther out to the NW (up to 53 dBZ, 26–34 miles away) — if any of those hold together and track in after the marine layer collapses near 8 PM, they would arrive with no local buffer and should be treated as a straight severe-thunderstorm threat, not a discounted one.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked cell 14 mi WNW closing at 23 kt; the marine layer is still fully standing at that arrival time and may push it late or weaken it.

wind.tactics_blurb: Fills SW-SSW through the afternoon and holds SW into evening as the gradient wind reinforces the sea breeze rather than fighting it — expect a brief gusty, shifty interruption right around 4 PM as a storm cell tracks by 14 miles out. Pressure is fairly even across the cove on this direction, with maybe a touch more breeze near the mouth and east shore; play it center-course and don't overcommit to either side.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a sea-breeze day reinforced by the background wind: air–water temperature difference (deltaT) is a strong 12.1°F, well above the 5°F threshold that gets a thermal circulation going, and the gradient wind is itself onshore — airport stations at Bridgeport and Westchester both show SW–WSW around 9–10 kt. Because the background flow and the thermal are pushing the same direction instead of fighting, the wind should run steadier and a bit stronger through the window than a pure sea-breeze day would.

HRRR's raw forecast direction was running well behind the real sea breeze at fetch time — model said SSW (193°) while western-LIS stations were already reading W (264°), a 71° gap. That's the known HRRR lag in resolving the afternoon clockwise veer of the western-LIS sea breeze, so the early hours in this table lean on the corrected/observed direction rather than the raw model output; by hour two or three the model's own forecast catches up into the same SW/WSW band anyway, which is why the hourly table converges there.

Cove geography: SW–SSW flow runs fairly clean and uniform up the cove's N–S axis, with only a slight edge in pressure near the mouth and the east shore (less shelter from Tod's Point on this direction). There's no strong side-of-course bias today — play the middle, don't burn distance chasing a shift that isn't really there.

Shift character: expect a persistent right-veering trend through the first couple of hours as the sea breeze finishes maturing (SSW → SW → WSW), then more normal oscillation once it's established by 17:00–18:00. The one wrinkle is the storm cell tracking through ~14 miles WNW around 4:09 PM — that can produce a brief outflow gust or direction kick that HRRR's smoothed hourly output won't capture; treat the 16:00 hour as the least predictable of the window.

On the water: 6–9 kt with gusts to 9–14 kt is the sweet spot for one-design dinghies all evening — no postponement-level lulls expected, and nothing so windy it threatens smaller boats. After sunset (8:01 PM) the sea breeze itself is done, but the surviving SW gradient keeps ~6–7 kt going rather than the wind collapsing to nothing, so a late race should still be sailable, just a notch lighter.

data_caveats: RAP CAPE unavailable — instability read from the OKX area forecast discussion text as a fallback.
Buoy 44040 / WLIS marine observations are about 73 minutes old — used as the latest available reading for water temp and the Sound-effect calculation.
The 21:00 hour draws on the HRRR extended outlook (f07), which carries lower confidence than the primary f01–f06 window.
